Use a longer PTSD symptom measure and clinical interview to confirm screening results and track symptoms over time. C

background.definition: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) involves the development and persistence of intrusive and avoidance symptoms, negative changes in thought or mood, and arousal/reactivity for at least 1 month following traumatic event exposure.

list.listitem: The lifetime prevalence of PTSD in the general population is 8% but is likely higher in primary care patients.
Seventy to 90% of primary care patients report at least one lifetime traumatic event.
illustrates PTSD probability associated with various traumatic events.
More than $3 billion was lost in productivity per year in the United States in 2000.
PTSD is associated with increased risk of suicide attempts (sixfold), depression, anxiety disorders, substance abuse, smoking, risky behavior, somatization, and all-cause dementia.
PTSD is associated with decreased use of preventive health services.
Trauma exposure involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence.

Trauma exposure may involve directly experiencing the event, learning of a traumatic event happening to a close family member or friend, or repeated extreme event exposure. Pretrauma risk factors: ongoing life stress; low social support; prior psychiatric disorder; female gender; low socioeconomic status; low education; low intelligence; ethnic minorities; past child abuse; other previous traumatic events; family history of psychiatric problems; or poor preparation for the traumatic event.
Peritrauma risk factors: severe trauma; interpersonal trauma; perceived life threat; extremes of age; community trauma (extent of); past peritraumatic dissociation.
Posttrauma risk factors: ongoing life stress; low social support; bereavement; major resource loss; children at home; women with distressed spouse.
Firearm injury survivors had a higher PTSD symptom levels over the course of the year after injury admission compared to survivors of all other injury mechanisms.

Learning theory: life-threatening fear is classically conditioned by event exposure; any internal (thought, memory, or emotion) or external (person, place, and thing) cue reminiscent of the event produces an intense "fight or flight" fear response. The person avoids cues that trigger fear. This avoidance maintains fear.

Cognitive theories: several variations of this model exist; all models suggest that severe trauma becomes represented in complex memory structures. The activation of these memories (by internal or external cues) triggers intense thoughts and emotions that are pathologic in that these thoughts and emotions cause personal discomfort and dysfunction.
Psychodynamic theory: traumatic memories overwhelm defense mechanisms. Repeated recall of the traumatic event with associated fear is an effort to understand the event in a less threatening way.

Biological dimensions: hyperactivity/hypersensitivity of catecholamine pathways and overactivity/oversensitivity of the central opioid pathways is seen. The amygdala and hippocampus dysfunction, with possible atrophy from overexposure to catecholamines, serotonergic dysregulation, glutamatergic dysregulation, and increased thyroid activity.

Pediatric patients with PTSD exhibit functional and structural brain abnormalities including reduced corpus collosum area and lower cerebral and intracranial volumes. Adults with PTSD do not show these findings.

Traumatic events can result in negative (PTSD) as well as positive (posttraumatic growth) psychological outcomes. People with high posttraumatic growth may also have PTSD symptoms which can be further impacted by age, trauma type, and time since trauma. Therefore, people showing posttraumatic growth may also need assistance for PTSD symptoms.
A systematic review of 19 studies suggests that genetic predispositions, hormonal influence, and gender roles all contribute to an increased risk of women developing PTSD.

Screening should focus on primary care patients at increased risk of PTSD (e.g., traumatic event exposure, mental health symptoms, unexplained physical symptoms, etc.) using a validated brief screening measure. B
Structured debriefing sessions do not prevent the advancement of ASD to PTSD. B
Early treatment with cognitive behavioral therapy may prevent the progression from ASD to PTSD. B

A civilian primary care based study contrasted the test performance characteristics of four commonly used PTSD symptom measures (PCL, SPAN, Breslau scale, PC-PTSD) against a PTSD diagnosis based on a modified Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS) interview. All PTSD symptom measures demonstrated adequate accuracy. The four item PC-PTSD was considered superior based upon both its brevity and test performance characteristics (optimal cutoff = 3; 85% sensitivity, 82% specificity).

The Injured Trauma Survivor Screen (ITSS) is a 9-item measure intended to predict future risk for PTSD and depression amongst injured adults admitted to the hospital. The ITSS has been shown to have adequate test performance to identify adults likely to develop PTSD (75% sensitivity, 94% specificity) or depression (75% sensitivity, 96% specificity) within one month of a physical injury requiring hospitalization. The ITSS continues to be a valid measure of PTSD at 1 to 3 months (75% sensitivity and 79% specificity, LR+ 3.6, LR- 0.32) and 6 to 9 months (73% sensitivity and 83% specificity, LR+ 4.3, LR- 0.33) post-injury across trauma centers.

International studies have identified risk factors associated with PTSD following traumatic event exposure (being female, low social support, physical injury related to trauma, intensity and duration of trauma exposure and loss of physical and psychosocial resources including one’s home. One Japanese study, found a PTSD rate of approximately 25 percent following an earthquake. Perceived loss of physical health and sense of community were associated with PTSD symptoms.
The Impact Event Scale-Revisited assessed at ICU discharge has a good ability for the detection of adult patients at risk of developing PTSD at follow-up (n = 145).
Early treatment with cognitive behavioral therapy may prevent the progression from ASD to PTSD.
Structured debriefing sessions do not prevent the advancement of ASD to PTSD.
A Cochrane review concluded that multiple session early psychological interventions may prevent PTSD, but the studies were generally at high risk of bias.
A nurse led package of interventions did not prevent PTSD in ICU patients; neither did patient diaries in the ICU.

Limited data is available on the efficacy of psychological therapies to prevent PTSD following trauma in adolescents and children however, based on the available data, psychological therapies can prevent PTSD and reduce symptoms following trauma for up to one month.

A Cochrane review of 13 studies concluded that the evidence was inconclusive regarding the use of early pharmaceutical therapy with SSRIs, gabapentin, propranolol, or other drugs for the prevention of PTSD.

There is no current evidence to support the use of a mobile phone application with self-help tools (PTSD Coach) to improve recovery after acute trauma among injured adult emergency department patients, though 76% of those who used it rated the app as moderately to extremely helpful.
Longer PTSD symptom measures can be used to confirm positive screening results and to track symptoms over time. B
Diagnostic confirmation is a clinical decision based on patient interview by a trained clinician. C
Reliable structured interviews exist to assist in making diagnostic decisions in difficult cases. C

Less severe stressful event; symptoms end within 6 months of stress resolution
Grief symptoms persisting at least 12 months after the death of a loved one (6 months for children)
Avoidance/numbing PTSD symptoms often mistaken for depression; can be comorbid
Excessive anxiety and worry that is difficult to control; somatic symptoms common
Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks with anxious apprehension; no index trauma
Stressful event may be extreme; psychotic symptoms persist at least one day and resolve in less than one month
Increases risk for trauma exposure and subsequent PTSD; may be comorbid
May increase risk for trauma exposure and subsequent PTSD; may be comorbid
PTSD encompasses posttrauma personality changes (e.g., withdrawal, distrust)

list.listitem: See for diagnostic criteria.

PTSD case-finding should focus on symptomatic primary care patients with known or suspected traumatic event exposure. Note that many patients will not be aware of the possible connection between traumatic events (particularly if distant) and current psychological symptoms.

More obvious presenting symptoms include depression, anxiety, anger/irritability, mood lability, substance abuse, sleep disturbance, and agoraphobic avoidance (not anhedonia) of previously enjoyed activities. Symptoms begin following a traumatic event. Symptoms presenting 3 months or longer after a traumatic event are likely to be persistent over time.

Patient may try to avoid internal (thought, memory, or emotion) or external (person, place or thing) cues that trigger their anxiety. Thus, these patients may initially appear avoidant, unmotivated, or "noncompliant."
Also elicit symptoms of possible comorbid mental health problems such as depression, other anxiety disorders, substance abuse, and suicidality.

A prospective longitudinal cohort study followed 150 dyads of Iraq and Afghan war veterans for 3 years. Self-reported difficulty controlling violence at baseline was an important predictor of subsequent violence, as was younger age, co-morbid PTSD, combat exposure, and having witnessed parental violence in childhood.
Diagnostic confirmation is a clinical decision based on patient interview by a trained clinician familiar with PTSD diagnosis.
Longer symptom measures may be helpful to follow up brief screening tests and to track symptom changes over the course of treatment.

Some trauma victims may have physical injuries (cuts, bruises, abrasions) or exposures (pregnancy, HIV, other sexually transmitted diseases) that require a medical workup. Selection of diagnostic tests appropriate to common posttrauma physical injuries and exposures is within the practice scope of primary care clinicians.
There is an association of C-reactive protein levels with PTSD symptoms, but the clinical importance of this association is unclear.

A systematic review examined the accuracy of clinical decision rules for PTSD in primary care and high risk populations. The Primary Care PTSD screener is a 4 item checklist that is practical in the primary care setting.
See algorithm in .
Psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral, cognitive processing, exposure based, and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) is the recommended first line therapy for PTSD. A
SSRI's are also effective, and can be used in conjunction with psychotherapy. A

A collaborative care model based out of primary care settings (case management, primary care provider, mental health consult) can be effective in reducing PTSD and other associated mental health symptoms.
B

Telehealth is a promising modality for delivering evidence based PTSD psychological treatment to persons experiencing barriers to mental health care.
B
A systematic review found that drug therapy reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression associated with PTSD.

SSRIs are considered first-line drug therapy for adults with PTSD , with NICE guidelines recommending venlafaxine and sertraline. A Cochrane review of 8 studies with 1078 participants similarly concluded that SSRI's are first line medical therapy for PTSD. Symptoms were improved in 58% of SSRI treated patients compared with 35% of placebo patients (NNT = 4 to 5). They found lower certainty evidence for mirtazapine and tricyclic antidepressants.

Twelve weeks is considered an adequate length for medication trial before changing the approach. When an antidepressant is judged to be helpful, it should be continued for at least 12 months before a gradual taper. Patients with an early response to sertraline are four times more likely to achieve good functioning at the end of treatment.
PTSD patients treated with high dose escitalopram tolerated and adhered to the treatment regimen with an associated decrease in PTSD symptoms at 6 months.
SSRIs are typically used in combination with psychological therapies.

Two small RCTs have demonstrated efficacy of repeated ketamine infusions in reducing symptom severity in individuals with chronic PTSD with a 0.5 mg/kg ketamine (NMDA receptor antagonist) infusion compared with a midazolam infusion (0.045 mg/kg).
Intranasal oxytocin (nonpeptide hormone) reduces the intensity of provoked PTSD symptoms in female patients with evidence inconclusive in male patients.

A systematic review of prazosin (alpha-1 blocker) for treatment of nightmares in children and adolescents with PTSD identified 6 case reports where prazosin treatment improved pediatric related nightmares indicating that further randomized control trials need to be conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of prazosin treatment for PTSD associated nightmares in the pediatric population.

A review concluded that prazosin can be effective for the treatment of PTSD associated nightmares as an adjunctive therapy in a veteran population. However, a large (n = 304) well designed RCT found no benefit in military veterans with chronic PTSD in terms of distressing dreams or sleep quality.

D-cycloserine (partial agonist of glycine recognition site of glutamatergic NMDA receptor) can augment the effect of exposure based CBT in anxiety, OCD, and PTSD regardless of concurrent antidepressant therapy.
In a randomized control trial conducted in a veteran population, quetiapine (atypical antipsychotic) treatment decreased PTSD symptoms of hyperarousal and re-experiencing as compared to placebo.
Cannabinoids have not been shown to be helpful.

Even after psychotherapy, PTSD remains a chronic illness with high rates of comorbidities. Within the past few years, there has been evidence to show the usefulness of various psychedelics such as ketamine and cannabinoids in the treatment of PTSD.

A RCT involving active-duty service members with PTSD symptoms showed that 2 right-sided stellate ganglion block (SGB) injections produced a clinically significant reduction in symptoms at 8 weeks (SGB n = 74, sham treatment n = 39).

Complimentary treatments for PTSD have been shown to be impactful on disease severity. Specifically, trauma sensitive yoga has been shown to decrease PTSD, depression and anxiety related symptomology in women who experienced interpersonal trauma. Trauma sensitive yoga created improvements in symptomology for women who were non-responsive to cognitive based psychotherapies. More significant reductions in symptoms were observed with extended duration of treatment.
Consider social and/or spiritual support for trauma survivors.

The 2019 APA guidelines recommend cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), cognitive processing therapy (CPT), cognitive therapy, and prolonged exposure therapy (in alphabetical order) as preferred approaches to psychotherapy for PTSD.

NICE guidelines recommend considering active monitoring or surveillance for those with mild or sub-threshold symptoms within one month of the trauma. For treatment of PTSD, psychotherapy consistent with APA guidelines above are first-line therapy, with venlafaxine or sertraline as the preferred drug therapy if selected.
A network meta-analysis of 12 with 922 participants providing 23 direct comparisons of psychotherapy and drug therapy concluded that psychotherapy was more likely to be effective.

listitem.strong: Cognitive behavioral and cognitive processing therapy

list.listitem: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (cognitive therapy, exposure therapy, and stress inoculation training) reduces PTSD rates compared with other forms of psychological treatment. This is best when given within 3 months, and is supported by NICE guidelines. A Cochrane review found 70 studies involving 4761 participants, and while studies were of low quality, trauma focused CBT, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), and non-trauma-focused CBT were all more effective than usual care.

A trial of 370 military personnel with PTSD randomized them to CBT with 10 sessions over 2 weeks, 10 sessions over 8 weeks, or a minimal contact control intervention. The more intensive sessions (10 over 2 weeks) were significatly more effective than control, and non-inferior to the less intensive intervention. Improvements were clinically significant.

CBT was associated with moderate symptom reductions in PTSD with effects still present after 12 months, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 randomized clinical trials of treatment for PTSD.

Cognitive processing therapy has been shown to be an effective tool at decreasing severity of PTSD, depression, and suicidal ideation for active duty military men through individual and group therapy sessions. Individual therapy resulted in greater reduction of PTSD severity.
Stress management and group trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are also effective.

Trauma-focused CBT and single-component trauma-focused interventions show positive effects long term (i.e., 6 months post treatment) at reducing PTSD symptoms when compared with control post treatment for idividuals with complex trauma.

In adults with comorbid PTSD and substance dependence, integrated exposure-based therapy was effective in a RCT of 103 persons. Treatment consisted of 13 individual 90 minute sessions with clinical psychologists.
A comparison of prolonged exposure and sertraline found improvements maintained over 24 months with both interventions, although patients preferred prolonged exposure.

A randomized trial in Afghan War veterans found that virtual reality exposure therapy was effective, but that adding alprazolam appeared to impair success rather than enhance it. A systematic review of studies of cognitive processing therapy and prolonged exposure confirmed their effectiveness in military veterans.

Mindfulness based therapy was more effective than person-centered group therapy at reducing PTSD symptoms in a group of 116 veterans. It was also successful at reducing pain, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms in a second trial.
Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy is effective in reducing PTSD symptoms.
Imagery Rescripting (ImRs) and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) effectively treat adults with PTSD from childhood experiences at 8-week post-treatment assessment (n = 155).

Primary care clinics can be used to deploy simple, evidence-based psychological treatments for adults in war-torn regions. Lay health workers delivered an intervention based on problem-solving and behavioral techniques to Pakistani adults resulting in significantly decreased anxiety, depression and posttraumatic stress symptoms.

Frontline therapists from a culturally diverse community setting can be trained in prolonged exposure therapy with an associated decline in PTSD symptoms for patients with complex trauma (v. person-centered therapy).

Socioeconomically disadvantaged pregnant women with depression and co-morbid PTSD who underwent Brief Interpersonal Psychotherapy, with the addition medications in some cases, showed greater improvement in their depression severity, PTSD severity and improvement in their functioning when compared to those who used the traditionally provided maternity support services. This suggests that using an integrated stepped care treatment model- or a risk stratified approach- in public health systems may be beneficial for high risk pregnant women with depression and PTSD symptoms.

A small randomized control study found that the use of a single session psychoeducation treatment for trauma exposed adults in an urban setting could result in further increased mental health service utilization and was perceived beneficial to those who received the treatment.
A brief 4 session coaching intervention produced subjective benefits among participants in the VA primary care setting compared with treatment as usual.
Educate asymptomatic trauma survivors and responders regarding normal psychological reactions (including expected time course of days to weeks) and appropriate coping techniques.

Evidence for the use of canine assistance for military veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder appears promising, but has not yet been fully validated in the literature due to a small number of low quality studies.

Alternative treatment approaches to managing PTSD utilizing technology to increase access to mental health have been increasing in number. One such approach was a 6 week online cognitive behavioral self-management course, DESTRESS-PC. Participants showed significant improvement at 12 weeks post intervention when compared to the usual care model. However, differences in symptom improvement disappeared at the 18 weeks follow up. Further research is needed to confirm the potential benefits of online cognitive behavioral self-management for PTSD symptoms.

Few trials have evaluated the efficacy of PTSD treatment for people with severe mental illness. Evidence is inconclusive on the role of trauma focused cognitive behavioral therapy in the treatment of PTSD in those with severe mental illness. A single trial on the efficacy of eye movement desensitization and reprocessing had a favorable effect on treatment outcomes however other studies have demonstrated no clear treatment effect with this treatment modality.

In families of patients with chronic critical illness, palliative care led sessions designed to be information and supportive did not reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression and may be associated with increased PTSD symptoms.

Collaborative care models have been shown to improve access to mental health care for those with depression, anxiety, PTSD, somatoform disorders, panic disorders and substance abuse disorders. Collaborative care models have been shown effective across multiple patient populations, including within the military through programs like RESPECT-Mil, which improved active military members access to mental health services for PTSD and resulted in clinical improvements in symptomology. A collaborative care model was applied within a primary care setting to soldiers returning from war. It was effective in reducing both depressive and PTSD symptoms.
A collaborative care model was used with acutely injured trauma survivors seen at a level I trauma center and resulted in fewer symptoms of PTSD and less alcohol abuse more than 12 months.

Telehealth provided exposure therapy can reduce depression and PTSD associated symptoms in a veteran population independent of previous exposure to technology. Treatment can be delivered safely if it is conducted with appropriate safety planning and in accordance with published telehealth guidelines for psychiatraic crises for telehealth providers. Therapy can be provided in the presence or absence of medication to augment treatment with associated high patient satisfaction and clinical improvement.

Home based telehealth mental health services including cognitive processing therapy can facilitate access to care in a racially and ethnically diverse veteran populations by reducing geographic and financial barriers to care and with reduced stigma associated with care.

A telehealth delivery system and care team can effectively provide PTSD care. A centrally assisted collaborative telecare (CACT) intervention at Walter Reed National Medical Center showed modestly improved outcomes in PTSD and depression compared with usual care models.

In a veteran population, participants in a randomized control trial of telehealth as compared to in-person therapy using prolonged exposure therapy and cognitive processing therapy were found to have no statistical differences in dropout rates from therapy although, those who dropped out from the telehealth arm were found to complete more sessions than the in-person therapy. Furthermore, those participants receiving in-person therapy were more likely to cite logistical reasons for discontinuation of therapy whereas those in the telehealth arm had a non-significant trend to citing increased discomfort with the more stressful components of exposure therapy. There was no statistical difference in the patient-provider relationship between the 2 treatment modalities.
Since PTSD typically has a waxing and waning course, continuity with a physician experienced in treatment of PTSD is important.
Periodically screen for PTSD symptoms, possible comorbid mental health problems, or other signs of PTSD-related functional impairment and intensity of therapy if problems are detected.
Refer if patient prefers another provider or additional services or if provider believes the patient's needs exceed what can be provided within the current treatment setting.
Also refer or hospitalize the patient if suicidal, for withdrawal from alcohol or other substances (for detoxification), or if uncontrolled psychotic symptoms are present.
PTSD can occur among seriously ill inpatients.

Rates of 10% to 32% have been reported in patients after the following events: myocardial infarction, cardiac surgery, ruptured cerebral aneurysm, transient ischemic attack or cerebrovascular accident, and breast cancer.
The lifetime prevalence of PTSD is 21% to 35% in childhood cancer survivors and 27% to 54% in their parents.
All parents of infants with complex congenital heart disease should be routinely screened for PTSD, and parents who screen positive for PTSD should be referred for counseling.
PTSD is a chronic mental health problem with symptoms that wax and wane over the years. B
PTSD has substantial comorbidity including: physical health problems, mental health problems, and functional impairment. B
Most US adults with PTSD never receive professional treatment; when treated, PTSD is most often seen in ambulatory primary care settings. C
PTSD patients typically have active symptoms for more than 20 years. Each patient has an average of 3.3 symptom episodes in their lives. Each symptom episode lasts approximately 7 years.

One large nationally representative sample found increased risk of the following problems among patients with PTSD: high school or college failure (30%), teenage pregnancy (30%), marital instability (60%), and unemployment (150%).

People with PTSD are at increased risk of developing the following mental health problems for the first time: depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety disorders, alcohol abuse/dependence, and other drug abuse/dependence.

A meta-analysis of studies concerned with anxiety and cardiovascular disease found a strong correlation between chronic anxiety and cardiovascular mortality. PTSD was associated with a higher rate of cerebrovascular accidents compared to other forms of anxiety. No significant association between anxiety disorders, cerebrovascular accidents, or atrial fibrillation was found. Mixed results were likely due to variation in study methodology and few studies assess cardiovascular events as a primary endpoint.

PTSD was found to be associated with a significant increase in risk of early incident TIA and ischemic stroke independent of established stroke risk factors, coexisting psychiatric disorders, and healthcare utilization. Sex moderated the relationship for adults with ischemic stroke but not TIA. The effect of PTSD on ischemic stroke risk was stronger in men than in women (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.47-0.86; P = 0.003), but no effect of sex was found for TIA.
Among US adults with PTSD, 38% receive treatment annually.
Of US adults with PTSD who undergo treatment, 75% receive this treatment in nonpsychiatric ambulatory medical settings.
PTSD patients who undergo appropriate treatment, typically experience meaningful symptom reduction and functional improvement.
Explain to the patient that you understand why most traumatized people do not discuss such experiences (that it can feel emotionally uncomfortable to do so).

Be calm, reassuring, and somewhat directive (to instill trust and hope). Tell them what you are going to ask (about traumatic events) and why it is important (it may impact on current and future psychological and physical well-being).

You should tell the patient that PTSD symptoms can be addressed with education, support, medication, and psychotherapy. Try to leave the patient with an understanding of their condition and its management to instill a sense of hope.
PTSD is often persistent for combat veterans and Holocaust survivors (among other groups).
Elderly patients with PTSD demonstrate impairment of learning, free and cued recall, and recognition memory.
Higher PTSD symptoms were associated with cognitive impairment in immigrant Asian/Pacific Islander adults (mean age of 77.5 years, n = 86).
In a longitudinal study of 32 subjects over the age of 65, it was shown that treatment of the elderly with CBT for PTSD led to lasting resolution of symptoms and an improvement in quality of life.
Four to 8% of US women experience physical abuse during pregnancy, which can lead to PTSD.
Primary care providers should therefore maintain a high level of suspicion for domestic violence directed at pregnant women.
The implementation of short-term Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) on pregnant patients showed that brief NET can be successfully and safely implemented during pregnancy.

A systematic review of 13 studies with 8 different interventions for PTSD treatment found t PTSD treatment in pregnancy is most likely safe, despite some questions about methodology of the studies. No adverse effects on the unborn child have been associated with trauma-focused therapy.

Current guidelines and clinical trials on treatment of PTSD in pregnancy remain very slim, however researchers have been able to extrapolate existing data from the non-pregnant populations while assessing safety of methods on pregnancy and breastfeeding. First-line treatment for PTSD in pregnant patients remains psychotherapy, however, pharmacotherapy is indicated in situations of resistant PTSD or other co-morbidities. Of the medication options, sertraline seems to have the most optimum safety profile in pregnancy and postpartum periods.
Delusional memories are common following an ICU stay in children.
In general, psychological treatment appears to be beneficial.
NICE guidelines recommend cognitive behavioral therapy for children with PTSD, with consideration of eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR). Drug therapy is not recommended.
Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy for children appears to have the strongest empirical support at this time.
A Cochrane review found 14 studies with 758 children, and concluded that CBT is effective for up to a year after treatment, with improvements in PTSD and depression scores.

In children who have been sexually abused, a Cochrane review found 10 trials of generally high risk of bias with 847 participants. They found the best evidence for CBT reducing PTSD and anxiety symptoms, although even this effect was modest.

CBT Grief-Help demonstrated maintained reduction in PTSD symptoms in children and adolescents with prolonged grief disorder. CBT Grief-Help is a manualized treatment based on a cognitive-behavioral model which includes exposure interventions, including imaginary exposure (telling the story of the loss event, elaborating painful aspects), in vivo exposure (visiting the scene of the death), and writing (writing a letter to the lost person about what is missed most). CBT Grief-Help included 9 individual sessions with children and adolescents paralleled by 5 counseling sessions with parents or caretakers.

Risk reduction through family therapy (RRFT) has been safely administered to adolescents with significant improvement in co-occurring substance use problems and PTSD criterion symptoms and with no evidence of iatrogenic effects (e.g., substance use problems exacerbation). RRFT is an adaptation and integration of evidence-based, cognitive-behavioral interventions that address PTSD symptoms (TF-CBT), substance use problems (multisystemic therapy), and sexual health.

A study involving the recruitment of 350 children in 2 cohorts investigated the efficacy of both the Screen for Child Anxiety-Related Emotional Disorders (SCARED) and a PTSD self-report measure by allowing child completion only in one cohort and both child and parent completion in the second cohort. Overall, the study showed significant differences between child and parental reports of symptomology. Overall, for PTSD evaluation in children, comprehensive assessment with both general and trauma-specific sequelae is recommended as children are not as open when completing certain screenings.

Emotional abuse is associated with more severe PTSD symptoms at the onset and over the course of treatment which bolsters the importantce of ongoing assessment of this at the onset of diagnosis as well as throughout treatment course.

algorithm.title: Management of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in the Primary Care Setting.a

cell.label: Patient at increased risk for PTSD
Routine care; consider rescreening in future if symptoms persist or worsen.
Provide primary care-based PTSD treatment: • SSRI • CBT or EMDR • Collaborative care model if available • Monitor response using longer symptoms scales.
Second-line treatments: • Other antidepressants • Anxiolytics • Mood stabilizers • Atypical antipsychotic • Other psychotherapy.
Consider referral or hospitalization if: • Patient preference • Patient needs exceed current setting • Suicidality • Alcohol or other drug withdrawal.

footnotes.footnote: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has several variants that are empirically validated as effective treatments for PTSD (cognitive therapy, exposure-based therapy, and stress inoculation therapy). From Practice guidelines ID #5187, 6850, and 5954; also Foa EB, Keane TM, Friedman MJ, eds. Effective Treatment for PTSD: Practice Guidelines from the International Society for Traumatic Stress Studies. New York: Guilford Press; 2000.

feature.caption: The Primary Care Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Screen (PC-PTSD).a
feature.feature_body:
1. Have had nightmares about it or thought about it when you did not want to? Yes or No
2. Tried hard not to think about it or went out of your way to avoid situations that reminded you of it? Yes or No
3. Were constantly on guard, watchful, or easily startled? Yes or No
4. Felt numb or detached from others, activities, or your surroundings? Yes or No
In your life, have you ever had any experience that was so frightening, horrible, or upsetting that, in the past month, you: aA cutoff score of 3 or more positive responses yields optimal sensitivity and specificity in primary care settings. Adapted from Prins A, Ouimette P, Kimerling R, et al. The primary care PTSD screen (PC-PTSD): development and operating characteristics. Prim Care Psychiatry 2003;9:9-14.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnostic Criteria Distinguishing Features
A. Traumatic event Exposure to actual or threatened, serious injury, or sexual violence (directly experienced; witnessed occurring to others; learning that a traumatic event had occurred to a close family member or friend; or, repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of a traumatic event).
B. Intrustive Symptoms (1 or more) Recurring distressing memories of the event; recurring distressing dreams of the event; dissociative reactions (individual feels or reacts as if the traumatic event is recurring); intense or prolonged psychological distress to internal or external cues; marked physiologic reactions to internal or external cues.
C. Avoidance symptoms (1 or both) Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings associated with the traumatic event; or, efforts to avoid external reminders linked with distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.
D: Negative alterations in cognitions or mood (2 or more) Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event; persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about self, other, or the world; distorted cognitions resulting in blame of self or others; persistent negative emotional state; markedly reduced interest in significant activities; persistent inability to experience positive emotions.
E: Arousal and reactivity (2 or more) Irritable behavior and angry outbursts; reckless of self-destructive behavior; hypervigilance; exaggerated startle response; problems with concentration; sleep disturbance.
F: Duration Symptoms persist more than 1 month.
G: Functional Impairment Social, occupational, or other important areas of function are disturbed.
H: Exclusion Symptoms not due to substances, medications, or another medical condition.
1- These diagnostic criteria apply to adults, adolescents, and children older than 6 years.2- Adapted from American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed. Washington, DC: American Psychiatric Association; 2013.
